newsitem.title: USA: Cuban lawman says U.S. fails to combat terrorism.
newsitem.headline: Cuban lawman says U.S. fails to combat terrorism.

text.p: Cuba's parliamentary leader said on Friday he was withholding evidence that proved the bombs that exploded in two Havana hotels last weekend were made in the United States because Washington was not "serious" about such issues.

"We will use the evidence in a way we consider most appropriate," said Cuban parliamentary president Ricardo Alarcon. "We don't have to give it to persons who we don't know are going to uphold the law or who might share it with their terrorist friends."
Two small bombs went off in the lobbies of central Havana hotels the Nacional and the Capri on Saturday, slightly injuring three people and breaking windows.
Alarcon was speaking to reporters at the Cuban Mission to the United Nations one day after leading a Cuban delegation in talks with U.S. officials to discuss migration.

"I reminded them that for a number of years we have provided the U.S. State Department with information and data on plans for actions similar to the actions that took place in the two hotels," Alarcon said.

He added that he had personally alerted high officials to a Miami television show featuring "anti-revolutionary" elements describing violent acts they had committed in Cuba. No action had been taken, he said.

Alarcon said he was specifically angered by the behaviour of U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns who said on Monday the Cuban government was "paranoid" for charging that Americans were involved in the bombings without giving proof.
"Nicholas Burns tried to take the blame away without having any evidence to do that," Alarcon said. "A serious person would have said that they were going to investigate as is their obligation."
Cuba and the United States have no diplomatic relations and have been political enemies since the 1959 revolution that brought Cuban President Fidel Castro to power.

Delegations from the two countries have been meeting regularly since they signed a September 1994 joint communique and a May 1995 agreement aimed at halting the flow of illegal immigration from Cuba to the United States.
Alarcon said the latest talks in New York, which ended on Thursday, were held in "a constructive environment" and "confirmed the common interest of both governments".
